title: How Herd Immunity Works
subtitle: Play with a live outbreak model and discover why vaccinating most people can protect everyone

intro.question: Why can vaccinating **most** people protect **everyone**, and why does “most” mean such different numbers for different diseases?
body: You will not be asked to memorise anything. Each step hands you a live model of an outbreak: sliders, switches, a crowd of simulated people, a town of households.

Before each experiment you predict what will happen, then watch. Guessing wrong is the point: surprises are where understanding starts. The numbers come from simple textbook models and typical estimates, so treat them as illustrations, not forecasts.

formulas.expr: z1 - (z1 - 1 + exp(-reff * z1)) / (1 - reff * exp(-reff * z1))
z2 - (z2 - 1 + exp(-reff * z2)) / (1 - reff * exp(-reff * z2))
z3 - (z3 - 1 + exp(-reff * z3)) / (1 - reff * exp(-reff * z3))
z4 - (z4 - 1 + exp(-reff * z4)) / (1 - reff * exp(-reff * z4))

steps.title: One case becomes many
body: An infectious disease spreads in **generations**. One sick person passes it on, those people pass it on, and so on. The number that matters most is how many people each case infects when nobody is immune: the ((basic reproduction number|R₀)), written R₀.
Suppose each case infects [[rZero]] others. Drag that number. Generation 6 then has {genSix} new cases, and the first seven generations add up to {firstSix} people.

visuals.title: Generation by generation
visuals.label: Generation {k}: **{value|int}** new cases
visuals.caption: Each dot is one new case. Replay the chain with the play button or scrub through it.

predict.prompt: Each case infects 2 people. What if each case infected 4 instead: how many times more cases would generation 6 have?

options.text: Twice as many, because 4 is twice 2
options.why: That is the straight-line intuition, but the doubling happens at every generation, not once. Six generations of “twice as many” compound into 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2.
Close to what you get by adding the extra cases up generation by generation, but chains multiply rather than add.
4⁶ ÷ 2⁶ = (4 ÷ 2)⁶ = 2⁶ = 64. A difference in R₀ is multiplied in once per generation.

predict.notice: Generation 6 now has **{genSix}** cases instead of 64. The chain multiplies by R₀ at every step, so a small difference in R₀ becomes an enormous difference a few generations later. That is ((exponential growth)).

steps.takeaway: Cases multiply by R₀ every generation, so outbreaks grow exponentially.

steps.title: Above one it grows, below one it dies
body: What if each case infects fewer than one person on average? Some do infect others, but more of them infect no one, and the chain gets shorter each generation.

The curve shows cases per generation for R₀ = [[rZero]]. The dashed line is R₀ = 1, where every case exactly replaces itself. The vertical axis is a ((log scale)): each gridline is ten times the one below, so steady multiplication draws a straight line.

predict.prompt: Set R₀ to 0.8. What happens to the outbreak over the generations?

options.why: Growth needs each case to be replaced by more than one new case. At 0.8, every generation is 20% smaller than the one before.

options.text: It levels off at a steady number of cases
options.why: Levelling off happens only at exactly 1, when each case replaces itself. That is the dashed line.

options.text: It shrinks every generation and dies out
options.why: Multiplying by 0.8 again and again heads towards zero: after 12 generations only about 7% of the starting cases are left.

predict.notice: With R₀ = {rZero}, generation 12 has only {pow(rZero, 12)|dp2} cases for every case you started with: the chain fizzles. On the log scale the line now slopes **down**. Everything hinges on whether each case is replaced by more or fewer than one new case.

challenge.prompt: Find the R₀ where the curve goes perfectly flat.
challenge.success: At R₀ = {rZero} every case replaces itself exactly once, so the line stays flat. This is the knife edge between growth and decline.
challenge.hint: Watch the gauge needle and the dashed line.

steps.takeaway: If each case causes fewer than one new case, the outbreak shrinks and dies out.

steps.title: Immunity breaks the chain
body: Vaccination doesn't make a disease less contagious. It takes people out of the chain. Picture one case meeting {contacts} close contacts: the vaccinated ones are protected, and only the unprotected ones can catch it.
So what drives the outbreak is the ((effective R)): R₀ times the share of people still unprotected. Right now [[coverage]] of people are vaccinated, so effective R is {reff}.

visuals.title: One case, one round of contacts
visuals.caption: Thicker, faster dots mean more people passing through that stage.

predict.prompt: R₀ is 3. Half the town gets a vaccine that always works. How many people does each case infect now, on average?

options.text: Still 3: the disease is just as contagious
options.why: Each contact is just as risky as before, but half of those contacts can no longer be infected. Contagiousness hasn't changed; the supply of people to infect has.
Half the would-be infections land on protected people, so 3 becomes 3 × (1 − 0.5) = 1.5.

options.text: 0: the vaccinated half stops it completely
options.why: Vaccines protect the people who get them. The unvaccinated half is still open, and a case still meets plenty of them.

predict.notice: Each case still meets {contacts} people, but only {exposed} of them are unprotected, so the chain now multiplies by **{reff}** instead of {rZero}. Vaccination lowers effective R, and effective R is the number that actually drives the outbreak.

steps.takeaway: Effective R = R₀ × the share of people still unprotected.

steps.title: The tipping point
body: Push coverage up and effective R falls in a straight line. At some coverage it crosses 1, and from then on every outbreak shrinks, even though not everyone is immune. That crossing is the ((herd immunity threshold)): 1 − 1/R₀.
For a disease with R₀ = [[rZero]], the threshold is {threshold}. Press play on coverage and watch the needle cross into the green.

predict.prompt: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known, with R₀ around 15. What share of people must be immune to stop it spreading?

options.why: Half is enough only for diseases with R₀ around 2. Each measles case would still infect about 7.5 others.
That works for R₀ = 4. With R₀ = 15, a case surrounded by 25% unprotected people still infects nearly 4.
1 − 1/15 ≈ 93%. The more contagious the disease, the closer to everyone you need.

predict.notice: With R₀ = {rZero}, effective R only drops below 1 once **{threshold}** of people are immune. Look at the line: it starts much higher and has much further to fall before it crosses 1.

challenge.prompt: Keep measles at R₀ 15 and raise coverage until outbreaks shrink.
challenge.success: Effective R is {reff}: below 1. At {coverage} coverage measles cannot sustain itself in this model town.
challenge.hint: Use the coverage slider or press play, and watch for the needle to enter the green.

steps.takeaway: Herd immunity starts when 1 − 1/R₀ of people are immune; for measles that is about 93%.

steps.title: Watch it spread
body: Formulas describe averages. Here are 220 people wandering a town square. Three arrive infected. Anyone who comes close to a case may catch it, and recovers after a while. Vaccinated people never catch it.
With R₀ = {rZero} and [[coverage]] vaccinated, effective R is {reff}. Each run is random, but a run always replays the same way; press the dice for a new one.

visuals.title: A town square of 220 people
visuals.caption: The strip underneath shows how the mix changes over time. Ringed dots are staying home.

predict.prompt: At 30% coverage plenty of people get infected. If coverage rose to 80%, what would you expect?

options.why: That would be true if a vaccine only protected the person who got it. But at 80% coverage effective R is below 1, so chains die out early.

options.text: Almost no one beyond the first few, including the unvaccinated
options.why: Effective R falls below 1: each case meets too few unprotected people to keep the chain going, so the unvaccinated are shielded too.

options.text: No real change: the unvaccinated still mix with cases
options.why: They still mix, but a case rarely reaches them, because most of the people it meets are protected.

predict.notice: At {coverage} coverage effective R is {reff}. The few cases rarely meet anyone they can infect, so chains break before they start. Look at the blue dots: most **unvaccinated** people never get sick. They are protected by the people around them. That is ((herd immunity)).

steps.takeaway: Above the threshold even the unvaccinated are protected, because chains of infection can't find a path.

steps.title: Averages hide pockets
body: Real towns aren't evenly mixed. People who skip vaccines often live near each other or share a school. Each cell below is a household, and infection jumps to neighbouring households.
Both versions have the same average coverage of [[coverage]]. The only difference is whether the unvaccinated are scattered or clustered in one district.

visuals.title: A town of 1,296 households
visuals.cell: if(row == 18 && col == 6, 1, if(u < if(clustered, if(col < 12, coverage - 0.3, coverage + 0.15), coverage), 3, 0))
visuals.caption: The first case appears in the west district, the left third of the town.

visuals.title: 100 towns, one national average
visuals.caption: Each dot is a town. Towns vary around the national average by about {spread}.

predict.prompt: Coverage averages 70% either way, just above the 67% threshold for R₀ = 3. Now the unvaccinated cluster together in the west district. What happens?

options.text: Nothing changes: the average is above the threshold
options.why: The threshold applies to the people who actually meet each other. Inside the cluster, coverage is far lower than the town average.

options.text: The outbreak takes hold inside the cluster, even though the average looks safe
options.why: In the west district only 40% are vaccinated, well below the 67% threshold, so the infection has a connected path through it.

options.text: Clustering protects the town by keeping the unvaccinated apart
options.why: It keeps them apart from the vaccinated, which is exactly the problem: it packs the unprotected people next to each other.

predict.notice: Same average, very different outcome. Inside the cluster coverage is only {coverage - 0.3|pct}, far below the {threshold} threshold, so the infection burns through the district. Herd immunity is **local**: what counts is coverage among the people who actually meet. The scatter makes the same point for whole towns.

steps.takeaway: Herd immunity is local: clusters of unvaccinated people can sustain outbreaks even when the average looks safe.

steps.title: No vaccine is perfect
body: So far every shot has worked. Real vaccines protect most, not all, of the people who get them. If the ((vaccine|vaccine effectiveness)) is [[efficacy]] effective, you need more coverage to reach the same protected share: threshold ÷ effectiveness.
Pick a disease and slide the effectiveness to see the coverage each one needs.

visuals.title: Coverage needed to stop spread
visuals.caption: Typical R₀ estimates: flu about 1.3, the original COVID-19 strain about 2.5, polio about 6, measles about 15. A red bar would need more than everyone.

predict.prompt: Measles needs about 93% of people immune. Suppose the vaccine works for 90% of the people who get it. What coverage would you need?

options.why: 93% must be **immune**, not just vaccinated. With a 90% vaccine, vaccinating 93% leaves only about 84% immune.
That is roughly the answer for the real two-dose measles vaccine, which is about 97% effective. At 90% it is worse.
93% ÷ 0.9 ≈ 104%. Even vaccinating everyone would leave too many people unprotected.

predict.notice: Coverage needed = {threshold} ÷ {efficacy} = **{critical}**. Even vaccinating everyone would leave measles room to spread. That is why measles vaccination uses two doses, about 97% effective together, and why measles is the first disease to return when coverage slips.

steps.takeaway: Coverage needed = threshold ÷ vaccine effectiveness, so for very contagious diseases every gap counts.

steps.title: Two towns, one virus
body: Put it all together. Two towns of [[population]] face measles (R₀ {rZero}) with a vaccine that is {efficacy} effective. Town A vaccinates 70% of people. Town B vaccinates 95%.
The model solves the ((final size equation)) to estimate how many people an outbreak eventually reaches.

visuals.title: Your town at the current coverage

predict.prompt: Your town starts like Town A. If it vaccinated 95% instead of 70%, how many people would catch measles?

options.text: About a quarter fewer, since coverage rose by 25 points
options.why: Proportional thinking again. Near the threshold, each extra percent of coverage breaks chains for everyone, so the effect is far bigger than the change.
Halving would already be a big win, but the real drop is much larger, because effective R falls from about 4.8 to about 1.2.
In this model the outbreak reaches about 32% of Town A but only about 2% of Town B: more than ten times fewer people.

predict.notice: At 70% coverage measles reaches about a third of the town; at {coverage} it reaches about **{infectedShare}**, roughly {infectedPeople} out of {population}. A 25-point rise in coverage cut infections more than tenfold, because it pushed effective R down to {reff}, right next to the tipping point.

challenge.prompt: Find the lowest coverage at which measles cannot take off in your town at all.
challenge.success: At {coverage} coverage effective R is {reff}: outbreaks fizzle. One percentage point lower and measles can spread again.
challenge.hint: Divide the 93% threshold by the vaccine's 97% effectiveness.

steps.takeaway: Near the threshold, each extra percent of coverage prevents far more than a percent of cases.

glossary.definition: The basic reproduction number: how many people one case infects, on average, when nobody around them is immune.
Growth by the same factor at every step, such as doubling each generation. It starts slowly and then explodes.
An axis on which each step multiplies by the same factor (here 10), so exponential growth or decline draws a straight line.
How many people one case infects right now, given the immunity already in the population. Above 1 an outbreak grows; below 1 it shrinks.
The share of people who must be immune for effective R to fall below 1. In the simplest model it is 1 − 1/R₀.
The protection that people who are not immune get when enough people around them are immune that chains of infection break.
The share of vaccinated people who are actually protected. A 90% effective vaccine leaves 1 in 10 vaccinated people unprotected.
z = 1 − e^(−R·z): in the simplest outbreak model, the share z of unprotected people that an outbreak with effective R eventually infects. The model solves it numerically.

wrapUp.heading: What you discovered
body: An outbreak is a chain, and every link multiplies by effective R. Above 1 the chain grows exponentially; below 1 it fizzles. Vaccination doesn't change how contagious a disease is. It removes links from the chain, and once enough links are gone, even people who could not be vaccinated are protected.
How many is “enough” depends on the disease: about a quarter of people for seasonal flu, over 93% for measles, and more again when vaccines are imperfect or the unvaccinated cluster together.
takeaways: Cases multiply by **R₀** every generation; small changes in R₀ make huge differences.
Outbreaks grow when **effective R** is above 1 and shrink when it is below 1.
Effective R = R₀ × the share of people still unprotected.
The **herd immunity threshold** is 1 − 1/R₀: about 93% for measles.
Herd immunity is local: clusters of unvaccinated people can sustain outbreaks.
next: Go back to the town square at 30% coverage and switch on “Half the town stays home”. How does staying home compare with vaccinating?
In “Averages hide pockets”, raise “How much towns differ” and watch more towns turn red with the same national average.
In “No vaccine is perfect”, find the lowest effectiveness at which polio can still be stopped.
